# Desire Paths

On almost any college campus or city park, you can find a thin brown line cutting diagonally across a lawn. It starts where the paved sidewalk makes an inconvenient right angle and ends where people actually want to go. Nobody designed it and nobody voted on it. It was made one footstep at a time by people who each decided, independently, that the official route was a little too long.

Urban planners call these *desire paths*, which is one of the more poetic terms to come out of a profession that also gave us "mixed-use zoning overlay." I think about them more than is probably reasonable.

What I love about a desire path is that it's a kind of honest data. A survey asks people what they want, and people answer with what they think they should want, or what they want on a good day. A desire path records what they actually did, repeatedly, when no one was watching and they were running late. It aggregates thousands of small, unselfconscious decisions into a single legible mark on the ground.

There's a story, possibly apocryphal, that some universities built no sidewalks at first. They planted grass, waited a year, and then paved wherever the grass had died. I've seen this attributed to Michigan State, to a campus in Finland, to the architect Christopher Alexander, and to various others. I suspect the real history is messier than the legend. But the legend persists because it describes a humility that's rare in design: the admission that the people who use a space might understand it better than the people who drew it.

---

The more common response is the opposite. The path appears, and a groundskeeper puts up a little fence, or a sign asking people to please use the sidewalk, or a row of shrubs. Sometimes this is justified. The shortcut might cross a fragile area, or there might be a reason for the official route that isn't visible from the ground. Designers aren't always wrong, and crowds aren't always wise; a desire path can lead straight into mud, or into traffic.

Still, the fence is usually a losing battle. People step over it. They wear a new path around the shrubs. The grass keeps dying. At some point, the question stops being "how do we stop this?" and becomes "why are we fighting this?"

I think this tension, between the plan and the worn path, shows up almost everywhere once you start looking for it.

Language is full of desire paths. Grammarians spent centuries insisting on "whom," and the language walked right past them. Contractions, dropped letters, and words that shift in meaning are the diagonal trails of speech. They form because they're shorter and easier, and because that's where people were going anyway. Dictionaries eventually pave them.

Software is full of them too. Every product team has had the experience of building a feature one way and watching users bend it into something else entirely. Twitter didn't invent the hashtag or the retweet; users did, and the company eventually built them in. Spreadsheets were designed for accounting and are now used for wedding seating charts, workout logs, and makeshift databases that run small businesses. That isn't misuse. It's a desire path.

Organizations have them. The official org chart says information flows one way, but everyone knows you actually ask Denise, because Denise knows. The formal process takes three weeks, so people have a workaround that takes two days. A smart manager studies the workarounds, because they show exactly where the official system is failing.

---

What interests me most is the moral ambiguity. A desire path is both a small act of defiance and a small act of collaboration. Each person who cuts across the grass is breaking a minor rule, but they're also contributing to a shared piece of knowledge. They don't coordinate. They don't even know each other. Yet together they produce something coherent, a line that's often startlingly efficient, closer to the true shortest route than any individual could have guessed.

There's something almost tender in that. The first person to walk across fresh grass leaves no mark at all. Neither does the second or the tenth. The path only appears after enough people have made the same choice, and by then no one can say who started it. It belongs to everyone who walked it, and to no one.

I find that a hopeful image. So much of what we build together is like this: traditions, slang, recipes, neighborhoods, norms of kindness or rudeness. None of these came from a single decision. They came from accumulation, from many people choosing slightly similar things for slightly similar reasons until the choice became visible.

It also cuts the other way. Bad habits wear paths too. A shortcut that saves thirty seconds can erode a hillside over a decade. The ease of a path is not proof of its wisdom; it's only proof of its ease. The trick, for planners and for people, is to tell the difference: to notice when the worn line reveals a genuine need the official design ignored, and when it just reveals that we'd all rather not take the long way, even when the long way is there for a reason.

---

The next time you see one of those brown diagonal lines across a lawn, it's worth pausing on. It's a map of collective intention, drawn without a pencil. It says: *many people wanted to go here, and the world wasn't built to take them.*

Sometimes the right response is a fence. More often, I suspect, the right response is to lay down some stones.
